As with the resolution to PHP’s sleep(), going with something that keeps things running unchanged for those who don’t move, but tailoring it further for those who want it, I’d opt for two extremes for logged-in users:
A: Adding a custom CSS styling text area, allowing for maximized creativity, experimentation, hacking, and freedom, and supporting any matter of taste and necessity. We have millions of dollars’ worth of CSS talent on this site and similar amounts of LLM investment to get something tasteful, respectful, well thought out, and just great. Make it a contest. This is not a dilemma, but I hope to inspire a move toward a native solution so I can read HN at night without the abracadabra of altering my OS, browser, trust, or, well, anything outside this site.

text:
Addressing EU Cyber Resilience Act

By Jacob Mammoliti, Solutions Architect, RapidFort
The EU Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) is a regulation (EU 2024/2847) that defines mandatory cybersecurity requirements for all products with digital elements sold in EU markets. Reporting obligations began on Sept. 11, with full enforcement commencing on Dec. 11, 2027. The CRA sets new requirements for teams working with containers and Kubernetes that impact how cloud native applications are built, distributed, and maintained throughout their lifecycle.
Cloud Native Environments and CRA Scope
Regardless of where a distributing organization is located, the CRA covers all container images, Kubernetes operators, and Helm charts with commercial support that are available to EU customers. The regulation specifies its scope as “products with digital elements” available in EU markets, and that also includes a lot of the cloud native stack.
CRA scope covers container images distributed publicly, commercial Kubernetes operators, open source with commercial backing, and Helm charts with commercial support. Open-source projects may also be impacted, including those with commercial backing or support contracts. In addition, the regulation requires a compliance chain throughout the cloud native supply chain.
CRA Requirements for Container Teams
The CRA introduces requirements that directly impact how teams build and operate container infrastructure. These categories include:
Vulnerability Management – SBOM data, continuous monitoring, and 24-hour ENISA reporting for exploited vulnerabilities.
Security by Design and Default – Hardened base images, minimal attack surfaces, and secure defaults as regulatory requirements.
Long-Term Security (5+ Years) – Ongoing security updates, rebuild pipelines, and backward-compatible patching for product lifetime.
This Act specifies that base images must be hardened with unnecessary components eliminated and secure configurations applied before products are made available on the market. The regulation orders what many in the cloud native community have long wanted – now minimal attack surfaces and secure defaults are regulatory requirements rather than recommendations.
As a result of the CRA, organizations must maintain Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) data, continuously monitor for vulnerabilities, and remediate within defined timeframes. Under the Act’s Article 14, actively exploited vulnerabilities must result in an early warning to The European Union Agency for Cybersecurity (maintaining the acronym from the agency’s previous name European Network and Information Security Agency – ENISA) within 24 hours of discovery, followed by a full notification within 72 hours. This mandates that organizations’ detection and incident response processes need to operate at scale across clusters.
Now products require security updates for a minimum of five years from the date of being available on the market, or throughout the expected product lifetime if that period is shorter, as stated in Article 13 of the CRA. For container teams, this requires tracking container versions deployed in customer environments, ensuring backward compatibility, and maintaining rebuild pipelines for older images – all while addressing security issues discovered years after release.

text:
Why the Creators of AI Do Not Understand Their Own Creations

Just citations.
Dario Amodei (CEO of Anthropic, 2025): "People outside the field are often surprised and alarmed to learn that we do not understand how our own AI creations work. This lack of understanding is essentially unprecedented in the history of technology."
MIT Technology Review: "Despite all the stunning success, nobody really knows how — or why — it works."
Yoshua Bengio (Turing Award laureate, 2024): "If we continue as before, we are driving against the wall. Or at least we are driving into a fog, without knowing whether there is a wall."
Mathematician Roman Vershynin (UC Irvine), in a recent interview — "We advanced to the wall and hit it."
So why did AI research hit the wall?
The answer is not hard to find, and most people in the field know it, even if they prefer not to say it loudly. The point is that all training data used by AI is secondary, while the primary source is the human being. Every text, every image, every pattern a neural network absorbs — all of it was created by humans. A neural network does not discover the laws of the world; it only finds regularities in what has already been created by human intelligence.
So if we want to understand how AI forms knowledge, we must first understand how humans form knowledge. But this pretty obvious idea was never materialized because of the historical failure of all attempts to build a working, mathematically correct model of knowledge. The story started in the 19th century and continued until the end of the 20th. Tens of theories of information, hundreds of books, thousands of articles in dozens of journals — and nothing practically working came out of it.
This however does not mean no adequate theory exists. It is there since the late 2000s, but it is still completely unknown to the scientific community. This occurs for a purely ideological reason because this theory builds its formalizations on concepts borrowed from mainstream programming languages and so completely ignores mathematics.
For the major journals devoted to AI and information theory that is a taboo. I spent years trying to publish it. The answer was always the same: "Add the mathematical justification, and then we will take a look." When I contacted established researchers directly, the answer was either silence or: "Yes, you have an original idea, but we are not interested."
I stopped trying fifteen years ago. My hope is that now the theory might have a chance, because it addresses exactly the problems that the current conceptual apparatus cannot solve.
The Theory of Meaningful Information (TMI) expands the conceptual framework of the most expressive programming language, which is C++, by adding capabilities for creating standard narrative (non-executable) texts that constitute the primary form of any human language.
In TMI, information is defined as the value of a variable used in some algorithm. This works for a bit in a computer, a state of a neuron, a pressed button, a written letter. It applies to a bacterium, a program, a neural network, and a human.
The theory introduces Information Capable Entities (ICE) and traces their evolution from the simplest biological ICE — a cell — to complex technical devices and the human being, who is modeled as an object controlled by a biocomputer (the brain).
It offers a complete algorithm of human knowledge formation, from the simplest perceptions to the most complex concepts. It contains the theory of intelligence, covering both natural and artificial intelligence, and the theory of a universal representation language.
A short description of TMI and a link to the complete work:
https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23403895
Boris Sunik,
independent researcher

text:
Anthropic Console overcharged my card 100x due to internationalization input bug

I am a LegalTech Attorney leading a developer team from Costa Rica. While trying to load credits onto my Anthropic API account (claude.com), I experienced a critical internationalization (i18n) and UX failure that has placed an unfair financial burden on me due to a severe oversight in their payment pipeline.
The platform prompted me for a payment. Since I am in a Spanish-speaking region where localized systems and keyboards handle dots and commas differently, I typed 5.04.
Anthropic’s input system completely failed to sanitize or validate the data. Instead of throwing a formatting error or converting it properly, it silently stripped the decimal internally and instantly charged my credit card $504.00 USD instead of $5.04 USD.
To make matters worse, there was no confirmation modal or review screen summarizing the final amount before processing the transaction. It was a single-click, instantaneous overcharge.
Anticipating the Obvious Skepticism:
Before anyone suggests "you should have checked your regional settings" or "just wait for the chargeback":
1. Users are not the QA team: In financial software, a system is never supposed to guess or automatically manipulate a numerical input without explicit validation. If an input is ambiguous due to locale differences, the application must reject it or ask for clarification, not execute a 100x overcharge.
2. Scale of the vulnerability: This time it was $504.00, which is an unfair and frustrating burden for independent developers. But because this pipeline completely lacks a confirmation screen and basic input sanitization, the exact same bug could happen to someone typing 50.00 and end up charging them $5,000.00 or more instantly. It is a systemic financial risk.
3. The Chargeback Illusion: Yes, I have already initiated a chargeback with my bank in Costa Rica. However, banking processes here are slow and take up to 120 days to resolve. In the meantime, the $504.00 has already been deducted and charged to my credit card statement. I am forced to pay for Anthropic’s engineering mistake out of my own pocket right now.
The Support Wall:
I filed an official complaint on the exact same day, minutes after it happened. I wasn't met with a human; I was blocked by an automated support BOT. The bot repeatedly and rigidly denied the refund, closing the ticket by citing generic policies without a single human ever looking at the fact that the overcharge was caused by a technical bug in their own platform.
As developers, we build systems that process people's money. Omitting a confirmation screen on a financial transaction, failing to sanitize localized numerical inputs, and then hiding behind unyielding AI support bots to keep money that doesn't belong to you is completely unacceptable.
If anyone from Anthropic's billing or engineering team is reading this, please look into this bug and review my case. It is a critical flaw that is actively harming international developers who are just trying to build on your ecosystem.
Pura vida!

text:
A misbehaving test MCP server for stress-testing your MCP client

We needed an MCP server that misbehaves on our command to test our own MCP gateway at work, but could only find well-behaved MCPs. That’s why we built a misbehaving MCP server ourselves and now share it on here, might be helpful for others building MCP gateways.
It’s similar to the MCP Inspector, but lets you test your client not your server.
We called it MCP Test Kitchen and it’s a (also hosted) MCP server that lets you:
* Connect any client that takes a URL and an Authorization header (Cursor, Claude Desktop or your own). It answers both 2025-11-25 and 2026-07-28 clients and logs which protocol revision each request declared.
* Pick one of 6 scenarios: HTTP transport errors, JSON-RPC error responses, tool results flagged isError, elicitation, multi round-trip requests (MRTR) via a C# SDK v2 scenario, and a baseline with a configurable delay. JSON-RPC and tool errors can be set to fail on a specific call, so the first call succeeds and the second fails. Resources and prompts are always on, each with a deliberately broken variant. If you want other scenarios, let us know.
* Watch every request in a live log with timing, method, caller, status and protocol version.
* Clone a TypeScript reference client, pinned to the latest spec, with full source.
You can run it yourself, it’s open source. If you’d rather test it live, we also hosted it, but you need to login (Google or GitHub, needed for the token) and can get started immediately.
We’d appreciate feedback, that’s why we're posting. In the live tool, there is a box that emails us directly. We’re around to check feedback + other scenarios you wish it had.
* Link to the repo here: https://github.com/cakewalk-security/cakewalk-mcp-test-kitch...
* Live tool access here: https://mcp-test-kitchen.cakewalk.security/login
* More information on why we built this: https://www.cakewalk.security/mcp-test-kitchen/blog/wtf-simu...

The result is that my homepage has been blocked for most of two weeks, my traffic has halved, and Google is indexing the warning page instead of my site. I've opened support cases and requested reviews each time. I've had one reply, on 5 October, and nothing on a lasting fix.
I'm not asking for special treatment. I'd like to know:
1. Is there a way to stop automatic mitigations from a reporter or text that has already been shown to be false?
2. Is there a manual-review setting for a domain?
3. Has anyone else seen the abuse form used like this, and how did it end?

Amateur radio operators are using 44Net Connect for everything from personal tinkering to club infrastructure, education, and emergency communications.
To get started, you’ll need a verified amateur radio call sign on the 44Net Portal: https://portal.ampr.org/. From there, you can sign up for 44Net Connect here: https://connect.44net.cloud.

text:
Ask HN: Are signed URL previews feasible?

Lots of protocols and software allow URL previews. But they have some annoying limitations:
For centralized public services the server can just retrieve the preview and serve it. But for decentralized services like Mastodon either every server has to fetch the preview on its own leading to lots of traffic and potential discrepancies between the previews served by different servers or the origin home server sends the preview but now everyone has to trust that it is authentic. The home server to which a link gets posted could place anything as its preview and thereby indirectly impersonate the URL and fake its content.
For E2EE messengers things are even more annoying because you do not want the servers to see the URL at all. So either all parties have to retrieve the preview on their own meaning they have to connect to a random, potentially malicious URL or only the sender does and everyone has to trust the sender that the preview is authentic which is a great opportunity for scams.^1
The perfect solution would be a standard for web servers to sign URL previews with their CA issued certificate. So that you can always proof that a preview is authentic. RFC 9421 already standardizes this. But this will not happen. There is virtually no chance of widespread adoption.
So my idea is:
You retrieve a webpage and record the whole TLS session including certificates, MACs and your key material like nonce and client random from the handshake. Now you use this as the basis for the URL preview. When you include your secret material from the TLS handshake anyone should be able to verify that the content is authentic from the server serving the URL due to the CA certificate and authentication of TLS traffic.
Standardize the request headers and limit the response length. Just cut off everything after the limit. Define some algorithm for computing the preview that ever recipient can verify. If you want to include linked images in the preview that increases complexity but should be doable. Repeat the whole thing with the linked image and create a bundle from all requests that authenticates the preview.
The downside I see is complexity and the need for the receiver to parse the preview bundle which might be attack surface.
Does anything similar already exist? Am I missing something or do you think this might be feasible to implement?
[1] Many messengers solve this by providing a URL preview service on the server. The client sends the URL to the messenger service which retrieves (and signs I hope) a URL preview which the client then includes in the message. This has the advantage that none of the parties of the conversation has to directly connect to an untrusted UTL. This bypasses E2EE for URLs. You can usually opt of this by disabling previews. Consider this if you did not know about this.

text:
JNISleuth-MCP – Recover Stripped JNI Bindings and Ollvm Branches for Ghidra/Ida

Hi HN, I’m a security engineer focused on Android anti-malware and reverse engineering.
When reversing hardened Android apps or wild malware, one of the most tedious parts is crossing the Java-to-Native (JNI) boundary when `.so` binaries are stripped, methods are bound dynamically via `RegisterNatives` inside an OLLVM-flattened `JNI_OnLoad`, and `JNIEnv` vtable calls decompile as raw pointer offsets like `(*(code *)(param_1 + 0x548))`.
I built JNISleuth-MCP to automate that workflow:
1. It parses multi-DEX APKs for `native` declarations and sweeps `.rodata` / `.data.rel.ro` (or section-header-stripped `PT_LOAD` segments) for `(char* name, char* sig, void* fnPtr)` triplets.
2. It statically resolves ARM64 OLLVM `CSEL` + `BR X8` indirect branches and `.rodata` jump tables in `JNI_OnLoad` (and can patch them in-place with direct `B.cond` / `B` instructions).
3. For runtime-packed samples that detect Frida, it includes a C++/NDK Dobby collector that hooks `RegisterNatives` mid-function.
4. It syncs the full 233-slot `JNIEnv*` vtable types and recovered C signatures into headless Ghidra and IDA Pro 9.0 (`idalib`/`idat64`), and exposes a model-agnostic MCP server + OpenAI/Gemini/Ollama tool schemas.
The repo includes a synthetic multi-DEX + stripped ARM64 `.so` crackme so you can test the entire pipeline in 30 seconds without needing a live malware sample. Would love feedback from anyone doing mobile RE or binary analysis!

I have had DNSSEC verification enabled for a couple of months in systemd-resolved. Not that I am particular paranoid or do any nuclear-sensitive stuff on my machine. Don't even own any Bitcoin. But mostly out of technical curiosity.

So I switched from DoT 1.1.1.1 @Cloudflare to DoT 8.8.8.8 @Google and life continued. Until today that suddenly out of nowhere showed the same symptom.
Turning off DNSSEC verification avoids the problem. An internet search brought up https://github.com/NordSecurity/nordvpn-linux/issues/1853 which also links to another one. The timing seems to match with my observation, but I don't use NordVPN. Any clues?
